core_principles.text: The anterior limb in both in-line and traditional lunges generates higher biceps femoris and gluteus maximus muscle activation compared to the posterior limb.

Vastus lateralis muscle activation remains similar regardless of whether an in-line or traditional lunge is performed, and does not differ significantly between the anterior and posterior leg positions.

specific_findings.text: In a study of 15 young, healthy, resistance-trained men (25 ± 5 years), biceps femoris activity was significantly greater in the anterior compared to the posterior position for the in-line lunge (p = 0.003) and the traditional lunge (p < 0.001).
Gluteus maximus activity was significantly greater in the anterior compared to the posterior position for both the in-line lunge (p < 0.001) and the traditional lunge (p < 0.001).
Medio-lateral balance was significantly greater in the in-line exercise in the anterior limb compared to the traditional lunge (p = 0.001).

core_principles.text: In a traditional lunge, the feet are positioned hip-width apart to distribute weight and maintain stability.
During the lunge, the forward knee should maintain a neutral alignment over the second metatarsal.
An in-line lunge variation positions the feet at 50% of hip-width apart, which narrows the base of support and increases the balance challenge.

specific_findings.text: The study's experimental protocol involved 15 young, healthy, resistance-trained men with a 10RM of 52.9 ± 14.4 kg in the traditional lunge.
In the study's specific lunge protocol, the forward knee was flexed to 45 degrees while the rear knee remained in full extension with both heels in contact with the floor.

consequences.text: Reducing the foot distance to 50% of hip-width apart narrows the base of support, which shifts motor responses to a hip strategy and increases stress on the hip adductors and abductors.

core_principles.text: The traditional lunge provides greater mediolateral stability compared to the in-line lunge.
The anterior leg in both traditional and in-line lunges experiences significantly greater activation of the biceps femoris and gluteus maximus compared to the posterior leg.
Stance width differences between traditional and in-line lunges do not significantly alter the activation of the vastus lateralis, biceps femoris, gluteus maximus, or gluteus medius.

specific_findings.text: Mediolateral balance displacement was significantly greater in the anterior limb during the in-line lunge (19.4 ± 4.1 cm) compared to the traditional lunge (14.8 ± 2.9 cm).
Biceps femoris activity was significantly greater in the anterior leg compared to the posterior leg for both the in-line lunge (53% greater) and traditional lunge (68.3% greater).
Gluteus maximus activity was significantly greater in the anterior leg compared to the posterior leg for both the in-line lunge (87.7% greater) and traditional lunge (88.3% greater).

consequences.text: Performing an in-line lunge increases mediolateral balance displacement, which increases the stability challenge during the movement.

core_principles.text: The lunge exercise requires coordination of both monoarticular and biarticular muscles across the hip and knee joints.
Both the anterior and posterior legs should achieve a knee joint range of motion of 0 to 90 degrees during the lunge.
A wider stance (traditional lunge) provides a more stable base of support compared to a narrower stance (in-line lunge), which demands greater mediolateral balance control.

specific_findings.text: The highest muscle activation in the anterior leg was observed in the vastus lateralis, reaching a delta percentage of approximately 53.4% in both in-line and traditional lunges.
The gluteus maximus showed lower muscle activity compared to the biceps femoris, with a delta percentage of approximately 6% in both lunge variations.
The knee joint range of motion is similar in both the anterior and posterior leg positions, spanning 0 to 90 degrees.
The in-line lunge showed 23.51% greater mediolateral balance demands compared to the traditional lunge.

consequences.text: A narrower base of support increases mediolateral instability, forcing the body to establish active muscular constraints to minimize joint degrees of freedom and stabilize excessive mobility.

Entering the sticking region of the lunge puts the anterior limb muscles in a poor mechanical force position where suboptimal muscle fiber length and myofilament overlap make it difficult to exert force.

core_principles.text: The anterior limb in a lunge generates higher biceps femoris and gluteus maximus muscle activation compared to the posterior limb.
The vastus lateralis shows similar activation levels between the anterior and posterior legs, as well as between the in-line and traditional lunge variations.
The gluteus medius acts primarily in the frontal plane of the hip joint to serve as a stabilizer during the sagittal-plane lunge movement.
The in-line lunge variation is recommended to challenge medio-lateral balance under load for balance or stability adaptations.

specific_findings.text: The anterior limb generated the highest biceps femoris and gluteus maximus muscle activation when compared to the posterior limb during the lunge.
The vastus lateralis showed similar activation between the anterior and posterior legs and between the in-line and traditional lunge exercises.
The in-line lunge showed greater medio-lateral balance when compared to the traditional lunge.
